items.item: A value's ownership only ever crosses a thread boundary at one of exactly four points in ordinary Rust: thread::spawn, thread::scope, tokio::spawn, or a channel send — never by merely sharing a reference across threads (that needs Send/Sync plus synchronization, covered in earlier topics, not an ownership transfer at all).

at.step: Four places, and only four, change which thread owns a value

items.item: thread::spawn's closure is a 'move' closure in practice: ownership of anything it captures by value transfers to the new thread, and the spawning thread can no longer use that data afterward.

at.step: Moved for good: the new thread owns it, the caller can't

items.item: thread::spawn's F: Send + 'static bound exists because the new thread may run for longer than the function that spawned it; without 'static, the closure could end up holding a reference to data that no longer exists.

at.step: Try to only borrow, not move, into a plain spawn

items.item: Trying to borrow (rather than move) non-'static local data into a plain thread::spawn is a real E0373 compiler error: 'closure may outlive the current function, but it borrows ... which is owned by the current function.'

at.step: Try to only borrow, not move, into a plain spawn

items.item: thread::scope relaxes the 'static requirement specifically because the scope function itself guarantees every thread spawned inside it is joined before the scope function returns — the borrow can never outlive the data.

at.step: thread::scope makes the identical borrow sound

items.item: tokio::spawn requires F: Future + Send + 'static, the same two constraints as thread::spawn, now expressed on a Future rather than a closure, for the identical structural reason: ownership and lifetime both need to survive a thread hop.

at.step: tokio::spawn asks for the identical Send + 'static contract

items.item: A spawned tokio task is not guaranteed to stay on the thread that spawned it; the docs state it may execute on the current thread or be sent to a different one depending on the runtime's configuration, which is exactly why Send is required at all.

at.step: Same contract, same reason: the runtime may move the task

items.item: std::sync::mpsc is a multi-producer, single-consumer channel: Sender (and SyncSender) are clone-able so many threads may send, but there is only ever one Receiver.

at.step: A channel send is the fourth crossing point

items.item: Calling send() on a channel moves ownership of the value out of the sending thread; the value only becomes reachable again once some thread calls recv() on the matching Receiver.

at.step: A channel send is the fourth crossing point

items.item: std::sync::mpsc's actual channel implementation (std::sync::mpmc internally) is not a bespoke algorithm; its own source comment states plainly that it is ported from the crossbeam-channel crate.

at.step: That channel's own implementation is borrowed, not built from scratch

items.item: Reusing crossbeam-channel's algorithm inside std is a deliberate engineering choice to adopt a mature, independently-tested design rather than maintain a separate, potentially-divergent implementation.

at.step: That channel's own implementation is borrowed, not built from scratch

items.item: None of the four crossing points are interchangeable: a plain spawn needs owned, 'static data; a scoped spawn trades that for a join guarantee; a task spawn needs the same ownership rule as a plain spawn; and a channel send is the only one of the four that doesn't involve thread::spawn or tokio::spawn at all.

at.step: Recap: where ownership crosses a thread boundary
